hazards.join-dots-as-straight-rule: You said the tide will keep rising along the same straight line. Your graph shows only the readings you took; a tide rises and falls again, and a line drawn past your last reading is a guess, not a finding.
hazards.lean-over-the-rail: You leaned over the pier rail to see the staff better. The rail is there because the drop to the water is dangerous; the technician's camera feed on the bench shows the staff close up, and you read it from behind the rail.
hazards.time-up-the-side: You put time up the side and height along the bottom. Time is what you chose to measure at, so it goes along the bottom; the height is what you found, so it goes up the side. Swapped axes turn a rising tide into a picture nobody can read.
hazards.uneven-axis-steps: You spaced the marks on the axis unevenly to make the points fit. Each step along an axis must stand for the same amount, or the graph's shape lies: a steady rise can look like a sudden jump and a jump can look like nothing at all.

interrupts.alert: A boat's wake sends a wave over the lower deck and the boards near the rail are wet.
interrupts.cue: Move back to the dry part of the deck and tell the technician the boards are wet.
interrupts.missNote: Nobody moved back, and a classmate slipped on the wet boards right beside the rail.
interrupts.why: Wet boards are slippery, and near a rail a slip is serious. Moving back and telling the technician lets them mark or dry the area; carrying on at the rail because the lesson is going well is how a small hazard becomes a fall.
interrupts.wrongNote: That leaves you on the wet boards. Move back and tell the technician. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: The harbour technician asks you to read out the staff as it is now.
interrupts.cue: Give the reading with its time and its unit.
interrupts.missNote: You gave a bare number with no time or unit, and the technician could not write it in the record.
interrupts.why: A reading without its time or unit cannot go in anyone's record. Saying all three together is the habit that makes your data usable by the technician, and it is exactly how readings are passed on at a working harbour.
interrupts.wrongNote: That misses the time or the unit. Give all three. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.ktp-checkin: The check-in comes at the very end of the visit.
lateNotes.ktp-tide-log: The tide record is written once every reading is plotted — nothing to record yet.

name: Graphing Tide Readings at the Pier

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Mark the three things you need before taking a reading from the tide staff.

decoyNotes.ktp-gull: Nice to watch, but it is not part of the reading.

itemNames.ktp-clock: the time on the pier clock
itemNames.ktp-scale-unit: the unit the staff is marked in
itemNames.ktp-waterline: where the water meets the scale

itemNotes.ktp-clock: Every reading needs its time, or it cannot be plotted.
itemNotes.ktp-waterline: Read at the water surface, looking level, not from above.

steps.prompt: Mark the three things you need before taking a reading from the tide staff.
steps.title: Find what the tide staff shows
steps.why: A tide staff is a tall ruler fixed in the water, and a reading means nothing without three things: where the water surface meets the scale, what unit the scale is marked in, and the time you read it. Taking all three together is what turns looking at the water into data you can plot.

steps.cue: Stand at the viewing rail before the technician switches on the staff camera.
steps.prompt: Stand at the viewing rail before the technician switches on the staff camera.
steps.title: Take your place behind the rail
steps.why: A pier is a working edge above deep water, and the rail marks where visitors stop. Taking your place behind it first means the whole lesson can happen without anyone near the drop, which is the same habit harbour workers keep when they work to the edge only with the right equipment.

steps.cue: Record the readings, draw the axes, choose an even scale, then plot the points.

itemNames.ktp-ord-plot: 4 · plot each reading as a point
itemNames.ktp-ord-table: 1 · record each reading with its time

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. Record the readings in a table before you draw anything.
steps.prompt: Record the readings, draw the axes, choose an even scale, then plot the points.
steps.title: Put the graphing method in order
steps.why: Recording the readings first, in a table with their times, means the graph is drawn from data and not from memory. Drawing and labelling the axes, choosing an even scale that fits the smallest and largest readings, and only then plotting each point keeps every point honest and the shape true.

steps.cue: Hold your view level with the waterline on the camera feed until the ripples settle.
steps.holdBreakNote: The view tilted and the reading jumped. Look level again and let the ripples settle.
steps.prompt: Hold your view level with the waterline on the camera feed until the ripples settle.
steps.title: Read the staff at eye level
steps.why: Looking at a scale from above or below makes the reading seem higher or lower than it is, which is called parallax. Holding your eye level with the waterline and waiting for the ripples to settle gives a reading that another person would agree with, and that is what makes data trustworthy.

steps.cue: Turn the axis dial until time runs along the bottom and height runs up the side.
steps.prompt: Turn the axis dial until time runs along the bottom and height runs up the side.
steps.title: Turn the graph to the right way round
steps.why: By agreement, the thing you choose to measure at goes along the bottom and the thing you find goes up the side. Following that agreement means anyone who picks up your graph reads it the right way first time, which is why every scientist and engineer draws time along the bottom.

steps.cue: Commit when the point sits exactly at the height the latest reading shows.

gauge.label: HEIGHT
gauge.missNote: Off the reading. Go straight up from the time to the height in your table.

steps.prompt: Commit when the point sits exactly at the height the latest reading shows.
steps.title: Plot the latest reading at the right height
steps.why: Plotting means finding the time along the bottom, going straight up to the reading's height, and marking there. Stopping exactly at the height the table shows, not roughly near it, is what keeps the line honest when the points are joined.

steps.cue: Drag the marker along the bottom to the time the reading was taken.

drag.missNote: Not at its time yet. Slide it along the bottom to the time in the table.

steps.prompt: Drag the marker along the bottom to the time the reading was taken.
steps.title: Place the point at its time
steps.why: A point sits where its time and its height meet. Placing it at the time the reading was actually taken, not at the next free space, keeps the gaps between readings true, so that a graph with readings taken at uneven times still shows the tide's real shape.

steps.cue: Say whether the tide was rising or falling across your readings, and how the graph shows it.
steps.prompt: Say whether the tide was rising or falling across your readings, and how the graph shows it.
steps.title: Say what the graph shows
steps.why: A line going up from left to right means the height grew as time went on; going down means it fell. Describing the pattern in words, and pointing to the part of the graph that shows it, is reading a graph rather than just drawing one.

steps.cue: Look at the draft graph and mark each problem.

decoyNotes.ktp-gr-title: A clear title is good practice. Keep it.

itemNames.ktp-gr-uneven: axis steps that are not even
itemNames.ktp-gr-wrong-time: a point at the wrong time

itemNotes.ktp-gr-no-label: Name the axis and its unit.
itemNotes.ktp-gr-uneven: Every step stands for the same amount.
itemNotes.ktp-gr-wrong-time: Check each point against the table.

steps.prompt: Look at the draft graph and mark each problem.
steps.title: Spot the problems in a classmate's tide graph
steps.why: Line graphs go wrong in a few familiar ways: an axis with no label, a scale whose steps are not even, and a point plotted at the wrong time. Spotting them on someone else's graph trains the eye that checks your own before it is shared.

steps.cue: Keep the marker on the waterline as the water moves up and down the staff.
steps.holdBreakNote: The marker lost the waterline. Follow the surface back and settle on its middle.
steps.prompt: Keep the marker on the waterline as the water moves up and down the staff.
steps.title: Follow the waterline as the tide moves
steps.why: Water in a harbour is never perfectly still, and a reading is the level the surface keeps returning to, not one splash. Following the waterline for a while shows why a technician takes the middle of the movement, and why one quick glance can be off.

steps.cue: Write each reading with its time and unit, and label the graph's axes and title.
steps.prompt: Write each reading with its time and unit, and label the graph's axes and title.
steps.title: Record the table and the graph
steps.why: The table is the evidence and the graph is the picture of it; keeping both lets anyone check a point against the reading it came from. Labelled axes, units and a title mean the graph still makes sense to someone who was not on the pier when the readings were taken.

steps.cue: Hold your graph beside the technician's own record and look for differences.
steps.prompt: Hold your graph beside the technician's own record and look for differences.
steps.title: Compare your graph with the technician's
steps.why: Comparing with an independent record is how scientists check their measurements. If both graphs show the same shape, the readings agree; if they differ, you look for the reason, a misread staff or a point at the wrong time, before trusting either one.

steps.cue: How did the readings and the graph go? What would you change next time?
steps.prompt: How did the readings and the graph go? What would you change next time?
steps.title: Check in at the end of the visit
steps.why: Ending with a check-in lets each learner say what made sense and what did not, and lets the teacher plan the next lesson around it. It is not a test; it is a moment to notice what you can now do with a graph, and a trusted adult is there if anything was hard.

supportLine: your teacher, a school counsellor or a trusted adult at home — if anything in this lesson was hard, talk it through afterwards
tagline: Time along the bottom, height up the side — and keep behind the rail while you read the staff
